Narrator: Part two. You will hear someone giving a talk. For each question, fill in the missing information in the numbered space. Write one word or a number for each answer. You now have some time to look at questions.
Narrator: You will hear a radio presenter called Erica, talking about how we can help the environment.
Erica: This morning, we're continuing to look at environmental problems, to see what we can do to help. And we can make a difference if we try. We often forget that as people who go shopping, we have a lot of power. If one company does something we don't like, we can always shop somewhere else.
Then there's the amount of plastic that comes with the goods we buy. Try buying things that aren't wrapped in it. And if you're offered a bag and you don't need one, just say, "No thanks." And any plastic bags you have at home, don't throw them away. Put them away somewhere until your next shopping trip and use them then.
On the subject of throwing stuff away, I try to keep things that other people might be able to use. There are always charity shops, which are very happy to help you recycle your old clothes or things in the house. Knowing that someone else is getting pleasure from something you no longer need is a lovely feeling.
Pollution is, of course, a big problem, and we often feel that as individuals, we have no power to make any difference, but that's not true. Find out what some of the local environmental problems are and see how you can help. Get together with friends and help to clear the rubbish from local rivers or collect litter from the streets around your home, to keep the area looking tidy.
Finally, let's turn to energy. Cars are here to stay for the moment, and it would be difficult to ask people not to use them at all, but we should all try to avoid making unnecessary car journeys. Go by bike or public transport sometimes, or if you work in the same area as your neighbor, try car sharing. Take it in turns to drive to work.

Speaker 1: My job is all about turning ideas into reality. I spend a lot of time sketching and choosing materials to create something that's not just clothing, but a statement. Last year, I designed a piece for a big event, and seeing it on the runway was one of the proudest moments of my life. Sometimes it's stressful because inspiration doesn't always come when you need it. But when it does, it feels amazing. I love seeing people express themselves through what I've created.
Narrator: Now, listen again.

Woman: Welcome to the Biology campus. I'm glad to have you here, and I'll be guiding you through the key facilities to help you familiarize yourself with the layout.
This campus has been designed to provide a well-rounded learning environment with everything you need within easy reach. We are currently standing at the main entrance marked by the black arrow on your map. Directly ahead, you'll see the receptionist's desk. This is the first stop for any questions or guidance you might need. The reception staff are incredibly helpful. So don't hesitate to ask them for assistance if you ever feel lost or need information. Now, if you look slightly to the lower left of the reception, you'll find the main hall. This is the heart of our campus, where students and staff come together for events, seminars, and other gatherings. It's a lively space, and you'll often find something interesting happening there. To the left of the main hall in the left corner of the map is the dormitory, which is where our resident students live. It's conveniently located, so you're never too far from your classes or campus facilities. Above the dormitory, there are two buildings, the gym and the kitchen. I always encourage students to use the gym to stay active.
It's a great way to take a break from your studies. And the kitchen? Well, it's the place to grab a bite to eat or catch up with classmates over lunch. Oh, and the fountain, which is in front of kitchen, is a lovely place to relax alone or with friends. Let's move to the right side of the map now. From the entrance, if you turn right, you'll find the administration office, where most of the administrative work is done, like course registrations and handling student inquiries. If you walk straight ahead past the reception's desk, you'll see a set of three vertically arranged rooms. At the top is the teacher's office, where you can find your professors if you need to discuss coursework or get extra help. Below that is the medicine room, a small but essential facility where you can receive first aid or medical attention if needed. Finally, at the bottom is the library, one of my favorite places on campus. It's a quiet, peaceful space filled with books, research materials, and study areas. I spent countless hours there during my student days. Lastly, on the far right of the campus, we have two specialized rooms. The upper room is the biology room, which focuses on biological research and records. I always find it fascinating to see the projects students work on there. Below it is the chemistry room, equipped for experiments and practical lessons. If you enjoy hands-on science, this will probably be one of your favorite spaces on campus. That concludes our tour of the biology campus. I hope this overview helps you find your way around.
Remember, everyone here is friendly and willing to help. So don't hesitate to ask if you need directions or support. Enjoy your time here, and best of luck with your studies.

parts.title: Part 6
parts.transcript:
Narrator: Part six. You will hear a part of a lecture. For each question, fill in the missing information in the numbered space. Write no more than one word for each answer. Mark your answers on the answer sheet. You now have some time to look at questions.
Speaker: My parents now both work from home, so they made the decision to move from our city center flat to the countryside, although it meant big changes for the whole family. It was a winter evening when we first went to the village, and as we walked along the pavement, I remarked on how dark it was without the streetlights of the city, and how bright that made the lights of the cars seem as they approached. I also noticed the sound of running water, and when we reached the house, I was delighted to discover that it stood next to a little bridge over a stream. I soon decided I liked the house. It has thick stone walls, high ceilings and wooden floors. The central heating keeps the temperature in all the rooms pleasant throughout the year, although during the colder months, those in the basement tend to get a bit damp, probably because of the stream. My room is actually on the other side of the house, so I don't hear it at night, which is a pity really. I was used to the constant big city background noise of traffic and voices, and for a while after we moved in, I'd keep waking up in the middle of the night, owing to the total silence there. It doesn't bother me now, though. And these days, I look forward to settling down for the night in my large, comfortable bed. I rarely stay up any later than when I was in the flat, and in the mornings, I normally wake up at the same time, but there aren't the sounds of the city telling you it's time to get up, so I'm usually in far less of a hurry to do so. The atmosphere here is so relaxing, and I have a wonderful view from the window of my room. Whereas before, I'd see city wildlife like cats, dogs, and maybe the occasional fox. Here, I start the day to the sound of distant farm animals and the sight of rabbits in the open fields. Apparently, there are also deer around, though I haven't actually spotted any yet.
The pace of life in the countryside is certainly slower, but I think I've adjusted pretty well to it. I must confess, though, that I can get a bit fed up with the speed of the internet connection here, compared with how fast it was in the flat downtown. In spite of that, I still manage to chat online with my friends there, more or less whenever I want. So I don't have the feeling of missing them that I thought I might have before I moved. There is, though, fairly weak mobile reception out here, sometimes no signal at all. And when that happens, I may not receive calls they're trying to make to me, which can be annoying. I suppose poor public transport is another disadvantage of living in the country. There isn't a railway station within 5 kilometers. It's nearly a 2 kilometer walk to get to a bus stop. And taxis charge a fortune to come out here. It's so different from where I grew up, where the buses stop right outside your home, or you can take the underground. You can live quite happily there without a car, but not here. People say, why not go by bike? But the reality is that it's just too far to ride anywhere from here, and dangerous on those country roads, especially in the dark. I'll just have to rely on my parents for lifts everywhere until I pass my driving test, which I hope will be before I go to university next year. Fortunately, it'll be a shorter drive from here than from where I used to live. And I'll avoid the awful traffic on the roads in and out of the city, too.
Narrator: Now listen again.

parts.passageContent:
Fiona says the lack of street lights in the countryside created a contrast at night.

Some rooms in the house can be rather _____(30)_____ in winter.

At first, the total _____(31)_____ made it difficult for Fiona to sleep in the house.

Fiona finds she tends to get up later in the day than when she was in the city.

In the countryside, Fiona sees _____(32)_____ from her bedroom window.

Fiona sometimes finds the slowness of the internet connection where she lives rather irritating.
